P00 / The question

Provisional abstract

Lower AI task costs can reduce the resource intensity of an operation while also making additional use attractive. Open-model catch-up may further change price, model routing, and who earns revenue from that use. This research proposes to examine those mechanisms together without equating a benchmark score, token price, or compute-expense ratio with useful-task or system efficiency.

The current draft sets out a source-addressable method, a bounded literature synthesis, distinct equivalency clocks, and a conditional demand–energy identity. The analytical identity shows why a break-even elasticity of one arises only under proportional price/intensity reductions and unchanged success/facility conditions. It does not estimate actual elasticity or demonstrate an Anthropic outcome. A text-based filing reconstruction supports four of the five initial financial figures and shows the fifth (aggregate commitments) was revised upward after the first amendment, with material conditional and excluded amounts; these remain unverified pending review. Empirical results, financial decomposition, release-pair distributions, and operational-impact estimates await acquisition, validation and review. Revise this abstract last when those results exist.

P01 / The question

The efficiency question and competing mechanisms

The consequential question is not whether a particular AI operation becomes cheaper. It is whether cheaper, more capable useful work reduces total resource demand or induces enough additional use to offset the improvement, and how benefits and burdens are distributed.

The provisional literature gives reasons to consider more than one regime. UKERC's indexed review description treats rebound as a factor in realized savings, not proof that efficiency cannot save energy (SRC-006, CL-008). Indexed text from Masanet and colleagues describes historical data-center compute growth outpacing energy growth (SRC-009, CL-015). These sources motivate both rebound and effective resource-conservation scenarios. Neither estimates frontier-AI elasticity today.

The proposed causal chain is technical/task efficiency → useful-task cost → price and product design → demand and workload mix → model/provider allocation → capacity and energy consequences. Each arrow needs evidence or an explicitly labeled assumption. The task-demand identity captures a direct response; spending elsewhere, capability change, and economy-wide effects require additional analysis.

The first supplied literature tranche sharpens what is missing rather than settling the question (tranche 01 S4). None of its seven sources measures or borrows an AI price elasticity. Rapid token growth is reported from vendor trackers (SRC-022, CL-046), but tokens are not tasks, and the same source lists ways those trackers overstate demand. The source's solvency corridor and scenario probabilities are outputs of assumed parameters, so they can structure a stress test but cannot calibrate one (CL-045).

Research backing: R01, tranche 01, W4 in PLAN §3. Full-text review and empirical AI-demand literature remain open.

P02 / The evidence

Evidence method and filing chronology

Anthropic is the proposed initial company anchor, conditional on authenticating primary documents. The source hierarchy favors filings and official disclosures, then independent research, with estimates and scenarios labeled separately. A claim described as “reported” is not automatically verified; classification, verification state, source confidence, and review status answer different questions.

The original S-1 and Amendment 1 are received text captures (SRC-001, SRC-002), alongside Amendments 2/3, the final prospectus and November 25 8-K (SRC-014–SRC-017). All six headers name the same issuer and CIK, with accessions and acceptance times matching the captured indices (CL-011). That is internal agreement, not authentication against SEC origin, which remains blocked by network access in the research environment.

The W1 reconstruction applies one declared pattern per fact to all five registration-sequence documents and records each value with its line locator, so a reader can see where a figure first appears, when it changes, and where a version left a placeholder. Derived checks recompute quarterly footings, rounded ratios, growth rates and the commitment decomposition; all 22 pass. The lineage matters: the original S-1 reports results only through June 30, 2026 and leaves every commitment amount blank; Amendment 1 adds the September quarter and first quantifies commitments; Amendment 2 revises the commitment total and adds termination and exclusion disclosures; Amendment 3 and the final prospectus leave the extracted facts unchanged. The 8-K covers closing, governance and placement items, not a new compute or revenue series.

Four of the five initial financial claims are supported by located passages (CL-001–CL-004) and one is superseded (CL-005, see P06). “Supported” is a reconstruction disposition. Every company claim keeps verification_state=unknown until origin authentication and a financial reviewer's sign-off are recorded; successive filings by the same issuer are not independent corroboration. Amendment 1's joined text is not used to assert table alignment.

P03 / The evidence

Decomposing efficiency without collapsing denominators

Financial ratios can change through pricing, product/revenue mix, accounting boundaries, procurement terms, utilization, or technical efficiency. The ratio of compute expense to revenue alone cannot distinguish those drivers, and is not a measure of gross margin unless the accounting definitions support that relationship. Company revenue cannot be converted to physical energy without workload and infrastructure evidence.

The filings illustrate the problem. The issuer reports compute and infrastructure expense falling from 251% of revenue in Q1-2025 to 48% in Q2-2026, then rising to 58% in Q3-2026 when $5.0B of short-term compute was delivered (CL-002, CL-003). It defines “compute efficiency” as intelligence produced and revenue generated per dollar of compute invested (CL-024). That is a financial and capability definition. The expense line covers research, model development, serving and internal use as one shared pool, and its composition widens in 2026 as leases and depreciation begin. The ratio therefore mixes revenue growth, prepaid capacity coming online, procurement terms and workload mix; it reports no task, token or energy denominator. It is evidence that financial efficiency improved during a ramp, not a measure of useful-task or physical efficiency (W1 §3).

The provisional task-energy literature describes different deployment costs across tasks and model configurations (SRC-005, CL-007). The appropriate denominator therefore includes useful output and quality, not just tokens or requests. For coding, test-defined issue resolution offers a candidate operational criterion (SRC-010, CL-016). Different task subsets and harnesses, including SWE-bench Verified, must not be merged into one supposedly comparable score (SRC-011, CL-017).

Inference-time compute makes the denominator harder still. A controlled evaluation of six frontier models found that larger token budgets added about 12 points on some benchmarks and about 0.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, and that repeated submissions raised scores everywhere (SRC-021, CL-040, CL-043). Success rate and energy per attempt are therefore set together by the reasoning budget and protocol; a falling price per token need not mean a falling price per successful task. Larger models in one distilled family did not give shorter correct answers (CL-044), and realized serving cost on identical hardware varied more than seventyfold with utilization (CL-048). Cost per successful task without protocol and serving metadata is not comparable (tranche 01 S2).

The proposed useful-task measures count failed attempts, retries, context and tools. They display success rate alongside cost and energy per successful outcome. Extraction and bounded-agent rubrics must be defined in advance; they cannot inherit a coding rubric by analogy. Draft rubrics for all three workloads, with every threshold marked as a proposal for reviewer decision, are in WORKLOAD-RUBRICS.md (0.4-draft, not adopted).

P04 / The evidence

What it would mean for an open model to catch up

The initial four-to-six-month hypothesis is testable only after specifying equivalency. Epoch's indexed analysis concerns an aggregate ECI gap, with a caution about public/private benchmark differences (SRC-004, CL-006). It is not an observed distribution of production substitutes for a particular Claude workload.

We distinguish benchmark catch-up, workload catch-up, and commercial catch-up. The second requires a matched task rubric and quality/cost configuration; the third adds licensing, serving availability, region, throughput, reliability and operational requirements. Open weights alone do not settle those requirements.

The benchmark clock is more fragile than it looks. Scores move with token budget, feedback, submission rule and parallel sampling, and 42 of 61 published evaluation citations do not record a token budget at all (SRC-021, CL-040, CL-042). Many published open-versus-closed score pairs will therefore be not comparable, a status distinct from matched or censored. Release type and licence also vary: in 2025, 47 of 102 notable models were released through API access, and 81 of 102 without training code (CL-051). Two supplied preprints assert open-weight parity without a stated method, and one relays a press claim that an open-weight model matches proprietary flagships at a fraction of the price (CL-047). These are leads, not measurements. No source in the tranche measures the lag, so CL-006 and the four-to-six-month hypothesis are unchanged (tranche 01 S1).

The release-pair investigation will retain frontier releases without a match by the cutoff as censored records. It will also record configuration and endpoint availability, rather than treating a model-release date as immediate commercial readiness. At present no release-pair dataset or equivalency distribution has been evaluated; no numerical lag finding is claimed.

P05 / The mechanisms

Demand response and the conditional rebound threshold

For a defined workload, use nonnegative price-elasticity magnitude e. With positive prices, the scenario demand ratio is (P1/P0)^(-e). This is a modeling assumption about price response, not a fitted relationship. Identifying real elasticity requires variation that distinguishes price from capability, customer growth, budgets, routing and other changes. A simultaneous price reduction and revenue increase does not identify it by itself. The filings show exactly that pattern: from Q2 to Q3 2026 revenue rose $5.4B while the issuer attributes an offset of about $600M to price reductions with new model versions and contractual discounts (CL-004). New models, products and customers arrived in the same quarter, so the observation is co-movement, not an elasticity estimate. The literature tranche adds named confounders for any future estimate: supply-injected volume, channel substitution, subsidies, low-value context re-reading, base effects, budget rationing and relocation from metered cloud to owned hardware. Relocation moves load out of a provider's revenue without removing it from the grid (SRC-022; tranche 01 S4).

Facility energy is expected attempted work times IT energy per attempt times matched PUE. Under the declared repeated-attempt model, successful task demand S and success rate s>0 imply expected attempts S/s. Combining these definitions gives:

E1/E0 = (P1/P0)^(-e) × (s0/s1) × (I1/I0) × (p1/p0)

If price and IT energy per attempt both decline by factor g, with 0<g<1 and success/PUE unchanged, E1/E0=g^(1-e). Thus the threshold e=1 is a conditional analytical result (CL-013), not a universal rule. Partial pass-through, quality changes, routing and changed facility intensity can move the boundary.

P06 / The mechanisms

Provider economics and committed capacity

Open-model substitution may change who serves a workload without reducing aggregate useful-task demand. A frontier lab could retain high-value tasks while losing repeatable price-sensitive traffic; conversely, product integration, governance, reliability and migration costs could slow substitution. These are hypotheses to investigate, not findings about Anthropic's realized margins.

Capacity economics must distinguish installed, available, contractually committed, and economically demanded capacity, with compatible units and delivery dates. Price pressure does not automatically imply insolvency. Cancellation rights, financing conditions, contract amendments, hardware usability, fixed obligations and realized utilization require contract-level evidence.

The initial research candidates are CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda and Crusoe for infrastructure, and Together AI, Fireworks AI and Baseten for managed inference. They are research cohorts, not a list of Anthropic counterparties or a ranking. Provider-specific disclosures remain acquisition tasks.

The final prospectus states aggregate contractual obligations and commitments of about $900.9B, substantially all compute and infrastructure, as of and after September 30, 2026 (CL-020). This replaces Amendment 1's $895.4B, which the initial draft carried (CL-005, superseded); the whole change is $5.5B of commitments signed after the quarter. Exposure is not one number. About $186.2B is subject to termination rights or contingent conditions, and an estimated $150–175B of variable arrangements is excluded from the total (CL-021). The named arrangements, including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, SpaceXAI, Broadcom and AMD, use different instruments, terms and conditions and must not be summed (CL-022).

Of the seven research candidates, only Lambda is named as a counterparty: about $41.3B of agreements into 2034, with fees only as capacity is delivered and accepted, of which an August 2026 agreement of about $34.9B is currently terminable by either party because Lambda did not secure a facility lease in time (CL-023). Nscale and Fluidstack are also named. The other six candidates are not named in these documents, which is not evidence that no relationship exists. This gives the provider chapter one evidenced, explicitly fragile edge, and shows why delivery and financing conditions matter more than headline totals (W1 §5–6).

P07 / The mechanisms

Operational energy, geography, and excluded impacts

Sector energy reports provide context, not a shortcut to company allocation. The indexed LBNL and IEA descriptions cover historical estimates and future scenarios, with different geography and inclusion of non-AI services (SRC-007, CL-009; SRC-008, CL-010). We have not inspected their full methods and do not insert their headline totals into the company model.

Operational electricity, historical emissions accounting, fixed-grid marginal response, and long-run effects of persistent load are different questions. Indexed EPA and Cambium records identify candidate methods, but annual inventory rates and long-run modeled rates are not interchangeable (SRC-012, CL-018; SRC-013, CL-019). Each calculation must disclose year, geography, units, factor type, grid assumptions, and coverage.

Unlocated capacity remains unlocated; US factors are not applied to non-US commitments. Direct cooling water is separate from electricity-generation water, and both are distinct from embodied/construction impacts. Missing factors produce unknowns or clearly labeled sensitivity scenarios, not zero impact.

P08 / The planned analysis

Deterministic futures: synthetic checks before empirical results

The first scenario families are efficient abundance, rebound acceleration, and demand air pocket / open-model substitution. They are not forecasts or calibrated probabilities. Their implementation must separate exogenous task demand, price response, model routing, success rates and physical intensity, without applying the same demand response repeatedly.

Before company calibration, the following checks expose the accounting logic (CL-014). Baseline desired successful tasks are 100, success rate is 0.5, IT energy is 0.01 kWh per attempt and PUE is 1.2. Baseline expected attempts are 200 and facility energy is 2.4 kWh.

P09 / The planned analysis

Uncertainty and reverse stress tests

Monte Carlo methods can propagate declared uncertainty but do not transform assumed distributions into measured event probabilities. Distribution choice, parameter correlations, seeds, failures, and model/data versions must accompany the results. No stochastic trials have been run for this paper.

The initial reverse tests investigate compute-cost pressure, committed-capacity mismatch, and regional power constraints. The two illustrative financial/capacity boundaries are expense above 60% of revenue and use below 60% of available committed capacity, respectively, for four consecutive comparable quarters. The regional boundary compares required load with documented deliverable supply in a matched period.

These are research triggers, not solvency, covenant, climate, or community acceptability certificates. Applying the compute-pressure trigger to the reported quarters shows why (CL-025): expense exceeded 60% of revenue in every 2025 quarter (251%, 177%, 148%, 144%) and in Q1-2026 (72%), so the four-quarter boundary was met during 2025, a period when revenue grew more than fivefold while committed capacity came online. Q2 and Q3 2026 were 48% and 58%. Crossing the boundary during a deliberate ramp is not a failure signal, and continuity across 2025–2026 depends on the composition change noted in P03 (W1 §7). The capacity-use and regional-power tests remain unevaluated: the filings disclose no utilization or facility-level supply. A search finding no breach within its domain is not evidence of safety outside that domain; claiming a minimal shock requires publishing the search method and admissible assumptions.

P10 / The implications

Distributional consequences and contestability

A useful task can benefit one group while shifting infrastructure burdens to another. The research therefore retains questions about affordability, water, land, noise, pollution and who participates in decisions, even where the initial quantitative boundary is operational electricity and emissions. Omitting an impact from a numerical total does not establish its absence.

Affected communities are participants who can contest sources, boundaries and acceptable tradeoffs, not merely constraints in a simulation. No stakeholder consultation or community-threshold agreement is claimed here. W6 must locate relevant evidence and review needs before drawing local conclusions.

P11 / The implications

Discussion, limits, and review questions

The present contribution is a bounded method and provisional synthesis, not an empirical verdict about Anthropic, neocloud viability, or total AI energy. The derived rebound identity supplies a conditional boundary, while the literature leads motivate multiple possible regimes and measurable workload definitions. Much of the central evidence remains to be acquired and inspected.

The first filing pass confirmed four of the five initial figures and superseded the fifth; later passes and review can still correct numbers or change the case-study framing. Failure to authenticate the anchor must produce an evidence-gap analysis, not a modeled company result. Failure of the six-month hypothesis is a valid finding. Future results should distinguish task price, workload growth, model substitution, provider allocation and facility intensity rather than report one efficiency score.

Still unknown after the first literature tranche (S7): any measured distribution of open/closed lags at any of the three clocks; open-weight results under protocols matched to frontier results; dollar cost and energy per successful task for any current model; whether token-efficiency gains offset rising test-time budgets; and any identified AI price elasticity.

Questions for review: Are the task rubrics defensible? Are the three equivalency clocks appropriately separated? Which causal links have identification evidence, rather than co-movement? Are financial/physical boundaries compatible? Can a reader trace every number through a source or formula? Which local impacts and participant perspectives are still missing?

Follow PLAN milestones and dependencies and the backlog to see what is unfinished. The author approved the revised specification and plan/backlog on 2026-11-28. Three actual reviewers and resolution of blocking findings are still required before analytical release.
